newsitem.title: USA: U.S. oil companies expand their spending horizons.
newsitem.headline: U.S. oil companies expand their spending horizons.

text.p: Cash-rich U.S. oil companies are gearing up for a spending spree from 1997 through the year 2000, chief executives and company presidents said at a industry conference in New York this week.

"We plan capital spending of $1.215 billion this year and similar figures through 1998 and 1999, a 43 percent increase on 1996," Victor Beghini, president of USX-Marathon Group's Marathon Oil subsidiary, said on Monday.

Marathon, an integrated oil major, will put $693 million into production this year and allocate $180 million for exploration to raise its output to 372,000 barrels of oil equivalent this year and to more than 400,000 barrels by 1999. The balance of the spending will go into its downstream operations.
Beghini expects a combination of increased activity and higher margins will double the company's profits by the next century from the $664 million earned last year.

John Seitz, Anadarko Petroleum Corp's senior vice president for exploration, said at the conference that his company aimed to produce 44 million barrels of oil equivalent in 1997 and 76 million a year by 2000, compared with 38 million in 1996.

The company, whose operations are focused on exploration and production, plans a 31 percent rise in capital spending in 1997 to $560 million, the highest in its history. Revenues in 1996 rose to $569 million from $434 million the previous year.

Last year, oil companies saw a direct boost to their bottom line from a rise in crude and natural gas prices. West Texas Intermediate benchmark blend crude rose to $22.14 per barrel from $18.43, and natural gas wellhead prices jumped to $2.41 per million Btus from $1.47.

Prices are expected to stay firm this year. PaineWebber, which organized the New York conference, forecasts a spot price of $21.50 per barrel for West Texas Intermediate in 1997 and $22 in 1998. It forecasts natural gas wellhead prices at $2.30 per million Btus this year and $2.15 in 1998.
The securities house acknowledges that its estimates are on the high side of analysts' expectations.
In addition to rising prices, energy companies have benefited from a decline in the cost of finding, developing and exploiting resources.

PaineWebber estimates that finding and development costs have fallen from more than $5.50 per barrel of energy equivalent in 1991 to a little more than $4.00 in 1995. Anadarko estimates its costs fell to $3.25 in the 1992-96 period from $4.92 in the 1988-92 period. Marathon costs fell to an estimated $3.26 in 1996 from more than $10 in 1992.
The industry has also benefited from restructuring.
Integrated oil major Texaco Inc has achieved gross savings of $3.2 billion since 1991 and its unit cash operating expenses have fallen from $6.20 per barrel of energy to $4.35.

Phillips Petroleum Co has cut controllable expenses from almost $3.0 billion to $2.7 billion in the same period. It is aiming to reduce its debt to between $3.0 billion and $3.5 billion from a peak of about $10 billion in 1988.
The reduced debt burden has allowed Phillips to budget $907 million for exploration and production in 1997.
To be sure, there are those who warn that the boom time may lead to a loosening of fiscal rectitude.

"We should also ask outselves whether the current period of prosperity will lead to another cycle of over-investment, followed by a downturn," H.L. Fuller, chairman of Amoco, warned a conference in Houston on Wednesday.
